locales:
  ru:
    title: "Что такое анемичная модель предметной области, чем она опасна и когда допустима?"
    prompt: |
      В проекте сущности вроде `Order` содержат только свойства с публичными `get` и `set`, а все правила
      (можно ли добавить позицию, как пересчитать сумму, когда заказ можно отправить) живут в классах
      `OrderService`, `ShippingService` и подобных. Как называется такой подход, чем он опасен и в каких случаях
      он всё же приемлем?
    hint: Кто может изменить свойство `Status` у такого заказа и кто проверит, что это изменение допустимо?
    answer: |
      - **Это анемичная модель предметной области.** Сущности - просто контейнеры данных без поведения, а логика
        вынесена в сервисы. По сути это процедурный код: структуры данных плюс функции, которые их обрабатывают.
      - **Инварианты не защищены.** Правила живут отдельно от данных, которые они охраняют. Любой код с доступом к
        сущности может написать `order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped` для неоплаченного заказа или добавить
        элемент в `order.Lines`, не пересчитав `Total`. Корректность держится на том, что каждый вызывающий не
        забудет пройти через нужный сервис.
      - **Правила дублируются и расходятся.** Одна и та же проверка повторяется в нескольких сервисах, со временем
        копии начинают отличаться, а чтобы понять, что вообще можно делать с заказом, приходится читать все
        сервисы, которые его трогают.
      - **Цена без выгоды.** Фаулер замечает, что такая модель несёт расходы модели предметной области
        (отображение на базу через ORM, отдельный слой), но не даёт её преимуществ.
      - **Альтернатива - богатая модель.** Сущность сама охраняет свои правила: свойства с `private set`,
        коллекции наружу как `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, конструктор, который не даёт создать невалидный объект, и
        методы с бизнес-смыслом (`order.AddLine(...)`, `order.Ship()`), которые проверяют условия и меняют
        состояние согласованно. Сервис приложения остаётся тонким: загрузить агрегат, вызвать метод, сохранить.
      - **Когда анемичная модель допустима.** Простой CRUD-сервис, где данные почти без правил проходят от формы до
        базы, а также модели для чтения, отчёты и DTO, у которых нет инвариантов. Там богатая модель добавляет
        церемонии и ничего не защищает. Выбор определяется сложностью правил предметной области.
    explanation: |
      Смысл объектной модели предметной области в том, что данные и правила, которые их ограничивают, находятся
      в одном месте. Если сущность сама не позволяет перейти в недопустимое состояние, нарушить инвариант можно
      только изменив её код, а не забыв вызвать сервис. В анемичной модели защита держится на дисциплине:
      достаточно одного нового места в коде, которое меняет свойства напрямую.

      Сервисы при этом не исчезают. Доменная служба нужна для логики, которая не принадлежит одной сущности
      (например, расчёт, затрагивающий несколько агрегатов), а сервис приложения координирует сценарий:
      транзакцию, репозитории, отображение в DTO. Проблема не в наличии сервисов, а в том, что сущности лишены
      всего поведения.

      Руководство Microsoft по микросервисам с DDD рекомендует богатую модель для сложной предметной области, но
      оговаривает, что для достаточно простого CRUD-микросервиса анемичная модель не является антипаттерном.
      Сильный ответ связывает выбор со сложностью правил: чем больше инвариантов, тем дороже держать их вне
      сущностей.
    linkTitles:
      - "Anemic Domain Model (Martin Fowler)"
      - "Проектирование модели предметной области микросервиса"
  en:
    title: "What is an anemic domain model, why is it risky and when is it acceptable?"
    prompt: |
      In a project, entities such as `Order` have only properties with public `get` and `set`, and all the rules
      (whether a line can be added, how the total is recalculated, when the order can be shipped) live in classes
      such as `OrderService` and `ShippingService`. What is this approach called, what is the risk, and when is
      it still acceptable?
    hint: Who can change the `Status` property of such an order, and who checks that the change is allowed?
    answer: |
      - **This is an anemic domain model.** Entities are plain data containers with no behaviour, and the logic
        sits in services. In essence it is procedural code: data structures plus functions that process them.
      - **Invariants are not protected.** The rules live apart from the data they guard. Any code with access to
        the entity can write `order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped` for an unpaid order, or add an item to
        `order.Lines` without recalculating `Total`. Correctness depends on every caller remembering to go
        through the right service.
      - **Rules get duplicated and drift apart.** The same check is repeated in several services, the copies
        diverge over time, and to learn what you may do with an order you have to read every service that
        touches it.
      - **Cost without benefit.** Fowler notes that such a model carries the costs of a domain model (mapping to
        the database through an ORM, a separate layer) without delivering its benefits.
      - **The alternative is a rich model.** The entity guards its own rules: properties with `private set`,
        collections exposed as `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, a constructor that does not allow an invalid object, and
        methods with business meaning (`order.AddLine(...)`, `order.Ship()`) that check conditions and change the
        state consistently. The application service stays thin: load the aggregate, call a method, save.
      - **When an anemic model is acceptable.** A simple CRUD service where data passes from a form to the
        database with almost no rules, and also read models, reports and DTOs that have no invariants. There a
        rich model adds ceremony and protects nothing. The choice follows the complexity of the domain rules.
    explanation: |
      The point of an object-oriented domain model is that data and the rules that constrain it live in one
      place. If the entity itself cannot be moved into an invalid state, the only way to break an invariant is to
      change the entity's code, not to forget a service call. In an anemic model the protection rests on
      discipline: one new place in the code that sets properties directly is enough.

      Services do not disappear. A domain service holds logic that does not belong to a single entity (for
      example a calculation that spans several aggregates), and an application service coordinates a use case:
      the transaction, the repositories, the mapping to DTOs. The problem is not that services exist, but that
      the entities are stripped of all behaviour.

      The Microsoft guidance on DDD microservices recommends a rich model for a complex domain, but notes that
      for a simple enough CRUD microservice an anemic domain model is not an anti-pattern. A strong answer ties
      the choice to the complexity of the rules: the more invariants there are, the more it costs to keep them
      outside the entities.
    linkTitles:
      - "Anemic Domain Model (Martin Fowler)"
      - "Design a microservice domain model"

fixedSource: |
  var order = new Order(maxTotal: 1000m);
  OrderLine line = order.AddLine("Keyboard", unitPrice: 100m, quantity: 5);
  try
  {
      order.ChangeQuantity(line, 20);
  }
  catch (InvalidOperationException)
  {
      Console.Write("rejected ");
  }
  Console.WriteLine(order.Total);

  public class Order
  {
      private readonly List<OrderLine> _lines = new();
      private readonly decimal _maxTotal;

      public Order(decimal maxTotal) => _maxTotal = maxTotal;

      public IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines => _lines;
      public decimal Total => _lines.Sum(l => l.UnitPrice * l.Quantity);

      public OrderLine AddLine(string product, decimal unitPrice, int quantity)
      {
          if (Total + unitPrice * quantity > _maxTotal)
              throw new InvalidOperationException("Order total limit exceeded.");
          var line = new OrderLine(product, unitPrice, quantity);
          _lines.Add(line);
          return line;
      }

      public void ChangeQuantity(OrderLine line, int quantity)
      {
          if (!_lines.Contains(line))
              throw new ArgumentException("The line does not belong to this order.");
          decimal newTotal = Total + line.UnitPrice * (quantity - line.Quantity);
          if (newTotal > _maxTotal)
              throw new InvalidOperationException("Order total limit exceeded.");
          line.Quantity = quantity;
      }
  }

  public class OrderLine
  {
      public OrderLine(string product, decimal unitPrice, int quantity)
      {
          Product = product;
          UnitPrice = unitPrice;
          Quantity = quantity;
      }

      public string Product { get; }
      public decimal UnitPrice { get; }
      // In a real solution the domain model is a separate assembly,
      // so only code inside it, such as Order, can change the quantity.
      public int Quantity { get; internal set; }
  }

locales:
  ru:
    title: Как изменение позиции заказа обходит лимит суммы в агрегате Order?
    prompt: |
      Агрегат `Order` не должен допускать сумму заказа больше лимита `maxTotal` (здесь 1000), и метод `AddLine`
      проверяет это правило. Строки 1-4 - внешний код приложения: он добавляет позицию на 500, затем меняет её
      количество, и программа выводит `2000`, то есть сумму выше лимита. Щёлкните по строке модели предметной
      области (строки 6-38), которая позволяет обойти инвариант агрегата.
    hint: Через какие члены внешний код может изменить состояние агрегата, не обращаясь к `Order`?
    answer: |
      Строка 37, `public int Quantity { get; set; }`: публичный сеттер позволяет изменить дочернюю сущность в
      обход корня агрегата, и `Order` не получает шанса перепроверить лимит суммы.
    explanation: |
      Агрегат - граница согласованности, а его корень - единственная точка входа для изменений. Инвариант
      «сумма не больше лимита» проверяет только корень, и только в тех методах, через которые идут изменения.
      Здесь проверка есть в `AddLine`, но количество позиции можно поменять напрямую: `line.Quantity = 20`
      меняет `OrderLine`, а `Order` об этом не узнаёт. Свойство `Total` просто пересчитывает позиции и
      возвращает `100 * 20 = 2000`.

      Строка 3 - лишь симптом: раз сеттер публичный, так может поступить любой код приложения, и инвариант
      держится только на дисциплине вызывающих. Возврат позиции из `AddLine` и свойство `Lines` сами по себе не
      проблема, пока через них можно только читать.

      Исправление - закрыть изменение количества для внешнего кода и добавить метод корня
      `Order.ChangeQuantity`, который вычисляет новую сумму, проверяет лимит и только затем меняет позицию. В
      исправленной программе изменение отклоняется, и выводится `rejected 500`. Модификатор `internal set`
      защищает позицию, когда модель предметной области лежит в отдельной сборке; в однофайловом примере
      внешний код находится в той же сборке, поэтому защита здесь условная. Тот же подход описан в руководстве
      Microsoft: дочерние `OrderItem` создаются и меняются только через методы агрегата `Order`, а коллекция
      наружу отдаётся только для чтения.
    linkTitles:
      - "Реализация модели предметной области микросервиса на .NET"
      - "Агрегат в DDD (Martin Fowler)"
  en:
    title: How does changing an order line bypass the total limit of the Order aggregate?
    prompt: |
      The `Order` aggregate must not allow an order total above the `maxTotal` limit (1000 here), and the
      `AddLine` method checks this rule. Lines 1-4 are external application code: it adds a line worth 500, then
      changes its quantity, and the program prints `2000`, a total above the limit. Click the line of the domain
      model (lines 6-38) that lets the aggregate invariant be bypassed.
    hint: Through which members can external code change the state of the aggregate without going through `Order`?
    answer: |
      Line 37, `public int Quantity { get; set; }`: the public setter lets code change a child entity without
      going through the aggregate root, so `Order` never gets a chance to re-check the total limit.
    explanation: |
      An aggregate is a consistency boundary, and its root is the only entry point for changes. The invariant
      "the total does not exceed the limit" is checked only by the root, and only in the methods that changes go
      through. Here the check is in `AddLine`, but the line quantity can be changed directly: `line.Quantity = 20`
      changes the `OrderLine`, and `Order` never learns about it. The `Total` property just recomputes the lines
      and returns `100 * 20 = 2000`.

      Line 3 is only the symptom: because the setter is public, any application code can do the same, and the
      invariant relies on the discipline of every caller. Returning the line from `AddLine` and the `Lines`
      property are not a problem in themselves as long as they only allow reading.

      The fix is to close quantity changes to external code and add a root method `Order.ChangeQuantity` that
      computes the new total, checks the limit and only then changes the line. In the fixed program the change is
      rejected and it prints `rejected 500`. The `internal set` modifier protects the line when the domain model
      lives in its own assembly; in a single-file snippet the external code is in the same assembly, so the
      protection here is nominal. The Microsoft guide describes the same approach: child `OrderItem` objects are
      created and changed only through methods of the `Order` aggregate, and the collection is exposed read-only.
    linkTitles:
      - "Implement a microservice domain model with .NET"
      - "DDD Aggregate (Martin Fowler)"

    title: Which statements about relationships on a DDD context map are true?
    prompt: |
      Select all true statements about the relationship types between bounded contexts on a DDD context map. The
      upstream is the context whose model others depend on, the downstream is the context that depends on it.
    hint: For each relationship ask who adapts to whose model, and who pays for the translation between the models.
    options:
      a: "In a conformist relationship the downstream context adopts the upstream model as is, without translating it into its own terms."
      b: "An anti-corruption layer translates the upstream model into the downstream model, so upstream concepts and changes do not leak into the downstream domain."
      c: "In a conformist relationship the upstream team adapts its model and API to the needs of the downstream team."
      d: "An open host service with a published language exposes one well-documented protocol and data format that many consumers use, instead of a custom integration for each consumer."
      e: "An anti-corruption layer is only justified in front of a legacy system; between two contexts that are being built now it is never needed."

    explanation: |
      A context map shows not only which bounded contexts exist in a system, but how their models relate, who
      depends on whom and where translation between models happens. A relationship type is a decision about who
      bears the cost of integration.

      - **Conformist:** the downstream gives up its own translation and uses the upstream model. Integration is
        cheap, but the downstream model is imposed from outside.
      - **Anti-corruption layer:** the downstream builds a facade or adapter that translates the foreign model
        into its own. This protects the domain, but the layer must be maintained and adds latency if it runs as a
        separate service.
      - **Open host service and published language:** an upstream with many consumers publishes one stable,
        documented protocol instead of separate integrations. Consumers can still put their own anti-corruption
        layer on top of it.
      - **Shared kernel:** a small fragment of the model shared by two contexts. It saves duplication at the price
        of constant coordination, so it is kept minimal.

      The choice depends on the relationship between the teams and on how valuable the downstream model is: for a
      core domain translation is usually worth it, for a supporting one being a conformist is sometimes wiser.

locales:
  ru:
    title: Что делать, если после команды пользователь видит устаревшие данные из асинхронной модели чтения CQRS?
    prompt: |
      Сервис построен по CQRS с отдельным хранилищем для чтения: команда меняет модель записи, а обработчик
      события асинхронно обновляет проекцию, из которой читают экраны. Пользователь переименовывает проект,
      страница перезагружается и показывает старое имя; если обновить её через секунду, имя уже новое.

      Почему так происходит, какие есть способы решения и чем приходится платить за каждый из них?
    hint: Что знает клиент сразу после успешной команды и как сторона чтения может сообщить, насколько она отстаёт?
    answer: |
      1. **Причина.** Проекция обновляется после фиксации команды, через очередь или обработчик событий, а запрос
         сразу после записи может прийти раньше. Это свойство согласованности в конечном счёте, а не случайная
         ошибка, и лечить его задержкой вроде `Task.Delay` перед перечитыванием нельзя.
      2. **Решать по экранам.** Обычно достаточно гарантии «читаю свои записи» (read-your-own-writes) для автора
         изменения, а остальные пользователи, списки и отчёты могут отставать. Допустимое отставание согласуется с
         бизнесом.
      3. **Вернуть результат из команды и обновить UI оптимистично.** Команда возвращает идентификатор, новую
         версию или итоговое состояние, и клиент показывает новое имя сам, не перечитывая проекцию. Цена: клиент
         дублирует часть логики отображения, при перезагрузке страницы или на другом устройстве проблема
         возвращается, а при асинхронном отказе нужен откат интерфейса.
      4. **Дождаться, пока проекция догонит версию.** Команда возвращает версию агрегата или позицию события,
         запрос передаёт минимальную нужную версию, и сторона чтения ждёт (или клиент опрашивает) с таймаутом,
         пока проекция её не обработает. Цена: проекция должна хранить версию или контрольную точку, растёт
         задержка ответа, а при сильном отставании нужен запасной путь.
      5. **Читать это одно представление со стороны записи.** Например, страница сразу после сохранения
         загружает агрегат из модели записи. Цена: дополнительная нагрузка на хранилище записи, две реализации
         одного представления и частичный отказ от смысла разделения, поэтому только для узких сценариев.
      6. **Честно показать, что изменение обрабатывается.** Статус «сохраняется» и обновление по push-уведомлению
         (SignalR, WebSocket), когда проекция готова. Цена: другой UX и инфраструктура уведомлений.
      7. **Синхронная проекция**, если модель чтения в той же базе: обновлять её в той же транзакции. Цена:
         запись медленнее, хранилища связаны, независимое масштабирование и перестройка проекций усложняются.
      8. **Наблюдать отставание.** Метрика лага проекции и алерт при превышении бюджета: иначе любое решение
         держится на предположении, что лаг всегда маленький.
    explanation: |
      Когда модели записи и чтения живут в разных хранилищах, их синхронизация занимает время, и документация
      Microsoft прямо называет это риском CQRS: данные для чтения могут не сразу отражать последние изменения.
      Фаулер отмечает, что раздельные модели ставят вопрос о том, насколько жёстко держать их согласованными, и
      часто приводят к согласованности в конечном счёте. Окно рассогласования нельзя убрать, не отказавшись от
      асинхронности, поэтому выбирают, кто и где его заметит.

      Ключевое наблюдение: строгая согласованность для всех обычно не нужна. Пользователя раздражает именно то,
      что он не видит **свою** правку, поэтому решения нацелены на сессию автора: клиент уже знает результат
      (оптимистичное обновление), знает версию (ожидание проекции) или временно читает из источника истины
      (модель записи). Каждый способ переносит цену в своё место: на клиент, на задержку ответа или на нагрузку
      стороны записи.

      Сильный ответ не предлагает одно универсальное средство, а выбирает его для конкретного экрана и называет
      цену. Слабый ответ - «добавить задержку» или «сделать всё синхронным», не заметив, что второе отменяет
      причину, по которой хранилища разделяли.

  en:
    title: What do you do when a user sees stale data from an asynchronously updated CQRS read model right after a command?
    prompt: |
      A service uses CQRS with a separate read store: a command changes the write model, and an event handler
      asynchronously updates the projection that screens read from. A user renames a project, the page reloads and
      shows the old name; if they refresh a second later, the new name is there.

      Why does this happen, what are the ways to handle it, and what does each of them cost?
    hint: What does the client know right after a successful command, and how can the read side report how far behind it is?
    answer: |
      1. **The cause.** The projection is updated after the command commits, through a queue or an event handler,
         and a query right after the write can arrive first. This is a property of eventual consistency, not a
         random bug, and it cannot be fixed with a delay such as `Task.Delay` before re-reading.
      2. **Decide per screen.** Usually the read-your-own-writes guarantee for the author of the change is enough,
         while other users, lists and reports may lag. The acceptable lag is agreed with the business.
      3. **Return the result from the command and update the UI optimistically.** The command returns the id, the
         new version or the resulting state, and the client shows the new name itself without re-reading the
         projection. Cost: the client duplicates part of the display logic, the problem returns on a page reload or
         another device, and an asynchronous failure needs a UI rollback.
      4. **Wait until the projection reaches the version.** The command returns the aggregate version or the event
         position, the query passes the minimum required version, and the read side waits (or the client polls)
         with a timeout until the projection has processed it. Cost: the projection must store a version or a
         checkpoint, response latency grows, and a large lag needs a fallback path.
      5. **Read that one view from the write side.** For example, the page shown right after saving loads the
         aggregate from the write model. Cost: extra load on the write store, two implementations of one view and a
         partial step back from the split, so only for narrow scenarios.
      6. **Tell the user the change is processing.** A "saving" status and a push notification (SignalR,
         WebSocket) when the projection is ready. Cost: a different UX and notification infrastructure.
      7. **Synchronous projection** when the read model is in the same database: update it in the same
         transaction. Cost: slower writes, coupled stores, and harder independent scaling and projection rebuilds.
      8. **Monitor the lag.** A projection lag metric and an alert when it exceeds the budget: otherwise every
         option rests on the assumption that the lag is always small.
    explanation: |
      When the write and read models live in different stores, synchronizing them takes time, and the Microsoft
      documentation names this as a CQRS risk: read data may not reflect the most recent changes right away.
      Fowler notes that separate models raise the question of how tightly to keep them consistent and often lead
      to eventual consistency. The inconsistency window cannot be removed without giving up asynchrony, so you
      choose who notices it and where.

      The key observation: strong consistency for everyone is usually not required. What annoys the user is not
      seeing **their own** change, so the options target the author's session: the client already knows the
      result (optimistic update), knows the version (waiting for the projection) or temporarily reads from the
      source of truth (the write model). Each option moves the cost somewhere: to the client, to response latency
      or to load on the write side.

      A strong answer does not offer one universal fix; it picks one per screen and names its cost. A weak answer
      is "add a delay" or "make everything synchronous", missing that the latter cancels the reason the stores
      were split.
    linkTitles:
      - "CQRS pattern"
      - "Martin Fowler: CQRS"

  en:
    title: A senior engineer proposes storing the state of every service as an event stream. What does the tech lead decide?
    prompt: |
      A senior engineer on your team proposes that, starting with the next project, every service stores its
      state as an event stream (event sourcing) instead of current-state tables. The arguments: a full history of
      changes, easy debugging and read models "for free". The next project is an order processing platform with
      several services: catalog, pricing, customer profiles, orders, payments, notifications and a couple of
      internal reference-data services. Most of the team has never built an event-sourced system.

      You are the tech lead. What do you decide, and how do you set its scope?
    hint: |
      Which concrete requirements justify the cost of event sourcing, and which services of this project
      actually have them?
    answer: |
      1. **Start from the problem, not the pattern.** Find out what is behind the proposal: audit requirements,
         resolving disputes, debugging, analytics over history. Separate real business or regulatory requirements
         from developer convenience.
      2. **Go through the bounded contexts.** Event sourcing pays off where you need a full change log as the
         source of truth, queries about the state at a past date (temporal queries), event replay and rebuilding
         new projections. Here the candidates are orders and payments, with their lifecycle and disputes. Catalog,
         reference data, customer profiles and notifications are mostly CRUD with few rules, and ordinary
         current-state storage is enough for them.
      3. **Name the cost openly.** Events are immutable and kept for years, so you need an event schema versioning
         strategy (new event types, upgrading old versions on read). Long streams need snapshots, projections must
         be rebuildable from scratch and their lag monitored. Read models are eventually consistent, and the
         current state cannot simply be selected with SQL. Replay must not call external systems again. Deleting
         personal data from an immutable log needs its own solution. On top come choosing and operating an event
         store and the team's learning curve. Backing out later is expensive.
      4. **Offer cheaper alternatives for the rest.** Change history: an audit table or database temporal
         tables. Integration between services: integration events through an outbox, which works without event
         sourcing. Separate read models: CQRS over an ordinary store.
      5. **Limit the decision to a pilot.** One justified context (for example orders); the other services store
         current state. The decision is recorded in an ADR: context and requirements, the decision and its scope,
         consequences, success criteria (change speed, projection lag, rebuild time, defect count) and exit
         criteria, plus a fallback plan: move to current-state storage by projecting it from the events.
      6. **Prepare the pilot.** The author of the proposal becomes its owner. Before the work starts, agree on
         event naming and versioning conventions, a snapshot policy, a projection rebuild procedure (tested in a
         test environment) and projection lag monitoring. Train the team and review the first aggregates in pairs.
      7. **Review against facts.** After the agreed period compare the results with the criteria. Extend the
         approach one context at a time and only with its own justification, never as a blanket rule for every
         service.
    explanation: |
      Event sourcing changes the storage model: the sequence of events becomes the source of truth, and the
      current state is derived from it. Fowler names the main benefits: complete rebuild of the state, temporal
      queries about any point in time, and event replay. He also describes the difficulties: during replay the
      interaction with external systems has to be disabled or substituted, and changes to code and event formats
      have to account for the history that is already recorded.

      The Microsoft guidance on the pattern lists directly where it is probably not useful: small or simple
      domains, systems with little business logic that naturally work as CRUD, systems where views of the data
      must be consistent and updated in real time, and systems that need no audit trail, history or ability to
      roll back and replay actions. It also notes that the pattern permeates the entire architecture and that
      migrating to it or away from it is costly.

      So a mandatory rule for the whole system is bad for two reasons. Technically, most services pay for the
      complexity without getting the benefit. Organisationally, a team without experience adopts the approach
      where mistakes are most expensive everywhere at once, and mistakes in the event schema stay in the log
      forever. A pilot in one context with an ADR and exit criteria turns a matter of taste into a testable
      hypothesis, keeps the engineer's contribution and limits the risk to one context.
    linkTitles:
      - "Event Sourcing pattern"
      - "Event Sourcing (Martin Fowler)"

  en:
    title: What does the RabbitMQ prefetch count limit, and what breaks when it is too high or too low?
    prompt: |
      Several instances of a service read one RabbitMQ queue with manual acknowledgements. Processing times vary
      a lot: most messages take milliseconds, but some take tens of seconds.

      What does the prefetch count set by `basic.qos` control? What goes wrong with a value that is too high (or
      unlimited) and with one that is too low, and how would you choose the value?
    hint: "Where are the messages that the broker has already sent to a consumer but the consumer has not acknowledged yet, and can another consumer take them?"
    answer: |
      1. **What prefetch limits.** `basic.qos` with `prefetch_count` sets how many delivered but not yet
         acknowledged messages a consumer may hold at once. When the limit is reached, the broker stops sending
         messages to it until an acknowledgement (`ack` or `nack`) arrives. A value of `0` means no limit.
         - In the .NET client this is `BasicQosAsync(prefetchSize: 0, prefetchCount: 10, global: false)` in
           `RabbitMQ.Client` 7.x (`BasicQos` in 6.x), called before consuming starts.
         - In RabbitMQ `global: false` means a limit per consumer on the channel, and `global: true` means one
           shared limit for the whole channel.
         - With automatic acknowledgements prefetch has no effect: a message counts as acknowledged when it is
           sent, and the broker sends messages without a limit.
      2. **Too high or unlimited.**
         - The broker hands messages to consumers that have free slots. An instance stuck on a slow message holds
           hundreds more in its buffer while other instances sit idle: the queue has nothing left for them.
         - Messages in the buffer wait for the slow neighbour, and their latency grows although free workers
           exist.
         - The queue counts these messages as unacked, not ready. Scaling on queue length does not trigger, and
           new instances only get what arrives later.
         - The buffer costs consumer memory, and under a heavy flow it may run out.
         - If the instance crashes or closes its channel, all its unacknowledged messages return to the queue at
           once and are redelivered with the `redelivered` flag: more duplicates and broken ordering.
      3. **Too low (1).** Distribution is as fair as it gets: a consumer receives the next message only after
         acknowledging the previous one, and work does not pile up at a slow instance. The price is throughput:
         a network round trip passes between an acknowledgement and the next delivery, so with fast messages the
         consumer spends most of its time waiting, especially when network latency is high. If the consumer
         processes messages in parallel, a prefetch below the degree of parallelism leaves some workers without
         work.
      4. **How to choose.**
         - Long, uneven tasks (seconds or more): 1 or a few, but not less than the number of parallel workers in
           an instance.
         - Fast, uniform messages: tens or hundreds, so that the buffer covers network latency. The RabbitMQ
           documentation calls the 100-300 range usually optimal for throughput.
         - A mixed workload is better split into separate queues with their own consumers and their own prefetch.
         - Send batched acknowledgements (`multiple: true`) before the consumer reaches the prefetch limit: if you
           wait for a batch larger than the limit, no new messages arrive and the consumer stalls.
         - Verify under real load: unacked messages per consumer, acknowledgement rate, processing latency and
           idle instances.
    explanation: |
      Prefetch is a flow control window between the broker and the consumer. A message sent to a consumer belongs
      to it until acknowledged: other consumers of the same queue will not get it, even if they are idle. So the
      window size decides how much work can get stuck at one instance.

      With uneven processing times a large window breaks the idea of competing consumers: work is assigned at
      delivery time, not when a worker becomes free. A small window assigns work by actual readiness, but every
      instance pays a network round trip for every message.

      The right value is the smallest one at which the consumer never waits for new messages. It depends on
      processing time, network latency and parallelism inside the instance, so it is measured, not guessed.
    linkTitles:
      - "Consumer prefetch in RabbitMQ"
      - "Consumer acknowledgements and publisher confirms in RabbitMQ"
      - "RabbitMQ tutorial for .NET: work queues"

    explanation: |

      уровень подтверждений задаётся свойством `ProducerConfig.Acks`, например `Acks.All`.

  en:
    title: How do Kafka acks and min.insync.replicas behave when brokers fail?
    prompt: |
      A Kafka topic has replication factor 3 and the setting `min.insync.replicas=2`. Producers write to it with
      different `acks` values. Select every true statement about what happens when brokers fail.
    hint: What exactly does the leader wait for with `acks=all`: every replica of the replication factor, or only the replicas currently in sync with it?
    options:
      a: "With `acks=all`, if one of the three brokers fails and drops out of the ISR, writes keep succeeding: the leader and the remaining follower are 2 in-sync replicas, which satisfies `min.insync.replicas=2`."
      b: "If two of the three brokers fail and only the leader stays in the ISR, the broker rejects `acks=all` writes with a `NotEnoughReplicas` error instead of acknowledging them with a single copy."
      c: "With `acks=1`, a record the leader has already acknowledged can be lost if the leader fails before the followers have copied it and a follower becomes the new leader."
      d: "With `acks=all`, the leader waits for all three replicas of the replication factor, so any single broker failure blocks writes until that broker returns."
      e: "`min.insync.replicas=2` also protects producers with `acks=1`: when the ISR shrinks below 2, the leader rejects their writes as well."
      f: "When the ISR shrinks below `min.insync.replicas`, consumers can no longer read the partition until the replicas catch up."
    optionExplanations:
      d: "The leader waits not for every replica of the replication factor but for the current set of in-sync replicas (ISR). A failed broker is removed from the ISR, after which writes are acknowledged by the remaining replicas again, as long as there are at least `min.insync.replicas` of them."
      e: "`min.insync.replicas` applies only to writes with `acks=all` (`-1`). A producer with `acks=1` is acknowledged right after the write to the leader's log, however many replicas are in the ISR."
      f: "The setting restricts only `acks=all` writes. Reads go through the leader and continue as long as the partition has a leader, even if only one replica is left in the ISR."
    answer: "Statements a, b and c are true."
    explanation: |
      The ISR (in-sync replicas) are the replicas of a partition that keep up with the leader. A follower is
      removed from the ISR when its broker fails or the replica lags for too long (`replica.lag.time.max.ms`).

      - With `acks=all` the leader acknowledges a write once every replica in the current ISR has it, not every
        replica of the replication factor. So once the failed broker is removed, writes continue.
      - `min.insync.replicas` sets the minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge an `acks=all` write. If
        that cannot be met, the producer gets a `NotEnoughReplicas` error (or `NotEnoughReplicasAfterAppend` if
        the ISR shrank after the write reached the leader's log). The error is retriable: the producer resends
        until `delivery.timeout.ms` expires.
      - The Kafka documentation gives replication factor 3, `min.insync.replicas=2` and `acks=all` as the typical
        durability setup: the cluster survives one broker failure without stopping writes, and with two failures
        writes stop, but no acknowledged record exists in a single copy. This deliberately trades write
        availability for durability.
      - With `acks=1` the leader answers right after writing to its own log. If it fails before replication, a
        follower without that record becomes the leader, and acknowledged data is lost. With `acks=0` the producer
        does not even wait for the leader.

      The setting changes nothing for `acks=1` and `acks=0` and does not affect reads. In the .NET client
      Confluent.Kafka the acknowledgement level is set with the `ProducerConfig.Acks` property, for example
      `Acks.All`.

      - "Apache Kafka documentation"
      - "Apache Kafka: KafkaProducer class"

  en:
    title: What can go wrong if you process the records of one Kafka partition in parallel and commit the offset of the last finished record?
    prompt: |
      To deal with growing consumer lag, a team receives the records of one partition with `poll`, hands them
      to parallel tasks and, whenever a task finishes, commits the offset of the record that finished last.

      What can go wrong in this design? How should offsets be committed when the records of one partition are
      processed in parallel, and what other consequences of parallel processing do you need to handle?
    hint: What does the consumer group assume about every record of the partition whose offset is below the committed one?
    answer: |
      1. **What a committed offset means.** The committed offset of a partition is the position from which
         the group continues reading after a crash or a rebalance. By convention you commit the offset of the
         *next* record, that is the last processed offset plus one. The group treats everything below that
         position as processed and will not deliver it again.
      2. **Lost records.** Records 100-109 are processed in parallel. Record 107 finishes, the team commits
         108, while 101 and 104 are still running. The process crashes or the partition moves to another
         consumer: reading resumes at 108, and records 101 and 104 are never processed. For them the guarantee
         becomes at-most-once, and the loss is silent, with no errors in the logs.
      3. **The offset can move backwards.** If 103 finishes next and the team commits 104, the position moves
         back, and after a restart the already processed 104-107 arrive again. The behaviour depends on the
         order in which tasks happened to finish, so it is hard to reproduce.
      4. **Ordering breaks.** Kafka guarantees order within a partition, and parallel tasks destroy it: an
         `OrderCancelled` event can be applied before `OrderCreated` of the same order.
      5. **Client thread safety.** `KafkaConsumer` is not thread-safe: the Java client throws
         `ConcurrentModificationException` when it is used from several threads. Worker tasks must not commit
         offsets; the thread running the `poll` loop does that.
      6. **Correct commits: by the contiguous prefix.** For each partition, track the dispatched and the
         completed offsets. You may commit only the watermark: the highest offset up to which *all* records
         are complete with no gaps, plus one (that is, the lowest unfinished offset). In the example above,
         while 101 is running you commit 101, even if 102-109 are done. The `poll` loop thread does the
         commit; tasks only report completion. In the `Confluent.Kafka` .NET client this is usually done by
         turning off `EnableAutoOffsetStore` and storing the watermark with `StoreOffset`, while auto-commit
         sends the stored offsets.
      7. **Bound the work in flight.** Keep an upper limit on the number of records being processed. When the
         buffer is full, call `pause` on the partitions and keep calling `poll`, so that
         `max.poll.interval.ms` is not exceeded and the consumer stays in the group, then call `resume`.
      8. **Rebalancing.** In `onPartitionsRevoked`, wait for the in-flight records of the revoked partitions
         and commit their watermark, or abandon them knowing they will be processed again.
      9. **A slow or poison record.** One stuck record holds the watermark back, and after a crash everything
         behind it is redelivered. You need timeouts, bounded retries and a dead-letter topic, and handlers
         must be idempotent: delivery is still at-least-once.
      10. **Ordering per key.** Parallelise by key rather than by record: records with the same key go to one
          sequential queue (by key hash), different keys run in parallel. This does not replace the offset
          watermark.
      11. **Try the simpler option first.** If ordering and simplicity matter more, increase the number of
          partitions and consumer instances, speed up processing, or process in batches. This keeps the
          standard commit model, but it changes how keys map to partitions, which has to be planned.
    explanation: |
      A Kafka consumer has no per-record acknowledgement: the group has only one number per partition, the
      position. That number implicitly states that every record before it is processed. A sequential consumer
      keeps that promise automatically, because records finish in order. Parallel processing breaks the link:
      the completion of a record with a higher offset says nothing about records with lower offsets.

      The `KafkaConsumer` documentation covers this in its section on multi-threaded processing: once you
      decouple consumption from processing, committing offsets manually becomes harder, because you have to
      know that processing for the partition is really complete. The watermark of the contiguous prefix is the
      only position that is safe to commit: a crash loses nothing, it only redelivers what was in flight, and
      the idempotent handler absorbs those repeats.

      The price of the design is complexity: offset tracking, backpressure through `pause` and `resume`,
      careful rebalancing, and more reprocessing when one record gets stuck. That is why a strong answer first
      asks whether adding partitions and instances is enough, and only then builds parallelism inside a
      partition.

      - "Apache Kafka: KafkaConsumer class"

    title: Find the line that makes undoing a command restore a stale font size
    prompt: |
      The editor starts with font size `12`. Two `SetFontSizeCommand` objects are created up front and then
      executed in turn: first size `16`, then `24`. After the last command is undone the size should go back
      to `16`, but the program prints `12`.

    hint: At what moment does the command remember the value that `Undo` will restore, and what was the editor state at that moment?

      `_previousSize` of each of them. Then `bigger.Execute()` sets `16`, `huge.Execute()` sets `24`, and
      `huge.Undo()` restores what the command captured at creation time, which is `12`. The state right before
      `huge` ran (`16`) is lost.

      before it changes the receiver. Any amount of time can pass between creating and executing a command:
      commands are queued, grouped into macros, or executed again after `Redo`. So the fix removes line 25,
      and `Execute` first reads `_editor.FontSize` into `_previousSize` and only then sets the new value. The

    title: Why is a static Singleton.Instance worse than a service with a singleton lifetime in DI?
    prompt: |
      In the first variant `PriceCalculator` calls the static `ExchangeRates.Instance`. In the second
      `PriceCalculatorDi` receives `IExchangeRates` through its constructor, and the implementation is
      registered in the container with `AddSingleton`. In both variants the application has one exchange rates
      object. What is the main drawback of the first variant?
    hint: Imagine a unit test of `PriceCalculator` - in each variant, how do you keep it from calling the real external API?
    options:
      a: Reading the static `Instance` property is noticeably slower than resolving a service from the container.
      b: "`PriceCalculator` has a hidden dependency on a concrete global object: the dependency is not visible in the constructor, and a test cannot substitute a fake for `ExchangeRates` without changing the class itself."
      c: A static Singleton cannot be made thread-safe, while a DI singleton is thread-safe automatically.
      d: "With `AddSingleton` the container creates a new `ExchangeRatesService` per request scope, so the second variant is not really a singleton."
      e: An object in a static property is never collected by the garbage collector, while a DI singleton is released after each request.
    optionExplanations:
      a: "It is the other way round: reading a static property is a plain field access, and resolving through a container does more work. But with constructor injection the service is resolved once when the object is created, and speed is not the issue here."
      c: "A static property initializer runs in the type initializer, which the runtime executes exactly once, so creating the instance is already thread-safe. And a singleton lifetime in DI does not make a service thread-safe: the documentation requires singleton services to be thread-safe themselves."
      d: "A new instance per scope is what `AddScoped` does. With `AddSingleton` the container creates one instance and hands it to every consumer."
      e: "A DI singleton lives long too: the root `ServiceProvider` holds it, usually until the application stops, and it is released together with the container. The two variants hardly differ in object lifetime."
    answer: "`PriceCalculator` has a hidden dependency on a concrete global object: the dependency is not visible in the constructor, and a test cannot substitute a fake for `ExchangeRates` without changing the class itself."
    explanation: |
      Both variants give one instance per application; the difference is how the consumer gets it. The call
      `ExchangeRates.Instance` is hard-wired inside the method: nothing in the signature of `PriceCalculator`
      says it calls an external API, and the only way to replace `ExchangeRates` is to rewrite the class. A unit
      test has to work with the real object, and if that object holds mutable state, the state outlives the test
      and leaks into other tests in the same process.

      In the second variant the dependency is explicit: `PriceCalculatorDi` receives the `IExchangeRates`
      abstraction, a test passes a fake to the constructor, and in the application the container with
      `AddSingleton` still creates one instance. So the singleton lifetime keeps the benefit of the pattern (one
      shared object) but removes the global access. Microsoft's DI guidelines explicitly advise avoiding static
      global state and using singleton services instead.
    linkTitles:
      - "Dependency injection guidelines in .NET"
      - "Singleton pattern (Refactoring.Guru)"

    title: How do you register a decorator in the built-in .NET DI container without third-party libraries?

      There is a `SqlProductRepository` and a caching decorator `CachingProductRepository` (code below).
      `IMemoryCache` is already registered with `AddMemoryCache()`, and `AppDbContext` is registered too. Which
      registration in the built-in `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` container (.NET 10, no Scrutor or
      other libraries) makes consumers of `IProductRepository` receive the decorator with a
      `SqlProductRepository` inside it?
    hint: How does the container choose an implementation when an interface has several registrations, and where does the decorator get its inner object from?
    options:
      a: "`services.AddScoped<IProductRepository, SqlProductRepository>();` followed by `services.AddScoped<IProductRepository, CachingProductRepository>();`"
      b: "`services.AddScoped<SqlProductRepository>();` and `services.AddScoped<IProductRepository>(sp => new CachingProductRepository(sp.GetRequiredService<SqlProductRepository>(), sp.GetRequiredService<IMemoryCache>()));`"
      c: "`services.AddScoped<IProductRepository, SqlProductRepository>();` followed by `services.TryAddScoped<IProductRepository, CachingProductRepository>();`"
      d: "`services.AddScoped<IProductRepository, SqlProductRepository>();` followed by `services.Decorate<IProductRepository, CachingProductRepository>();`"
    optionExplanations:
      a: "With several registrations of one interface, a single dependency resolves to the last one, which is `CachingProductRepository`. Its constructor needs an `IProductRepository`, and the container picks the same `CachingProductRepository` again: this is a circular dependency, and resolving the service fails with `InvalidOperationException`."
      c: "`TryAddScoped` adds the registration only if the service type has no registration yet. `IProductRepository` is already registered, so the call does nothing, and consumers get `SqlProductRepository` without the cache."
      d: "The built-in container has no `Decorate` method on `IServiceCollection`. It is an extension from the third-party Scrutor library, and without it the code does not compile."
    answer: "Register `SqlProductRepository` as a concrete type, and register `IProductRepository` with a factory that resolves `SqlProductRepository` from the container and wraps it in `CachingProductRepository`."
    explanation: |
      The built-in container in .NET 10 has no decorator API. When one interface has several registrations, a
      single injected dependency gets the last one, and the decorator's constructor asks for the very interface
      it implements. So the inner object has to be registered under a different key, most often its concrete
      type `SqlProductRepository`, and the interface is registered with a factory that builds the wrapper by hand.

      This approach has costs worth keeping in mind:

      - `SqlProductRepository` stays resolvable directly, and a class that asks for the concrete type bypasses
        the cache;
      - the decorator's lifetime must not be longer than the inner object's lifetime, otherwise a scoped
        repository holding a `DbContext` gets captured by a singleton decorator;
      - when the decorator gains new dependencies, the factory has to be edited by hand.

      Since .NET 8 the inner object can also be registered as a keyed service
      (`AddKeyedScoped<IProductRepository, SqlProductRepository>("inner")`) and resolved in the factory with
      `GetRequiredKeyedService<IProductRepository>("inner")`. Then the inner implementation is not exposed by its
      concrete type. When there are many decorators, teams usually add Scrutor for its `Decorate` method.

      - "Dependency injection in .NET"
      - "ServiceCollectionDescriptorExtensions.TryAddScoped method"

    answer: "0 3"
    explanation: |
      Декоратор перехватывает только те вызовы, которые приходят через ссылку на него самого. Вызов
      `repo.GetAll()` попадает в `CountingRepository.GetAll`, а тот передаёт его в `_inner.GetAll()`. Дальше

      внутреннего объекта становится `3`.

      Это ограничение композиции: обёрнутый объект не знает о своей обёртке, и его внутренние вызовы самого
      себя проходят мимо неё. На практике это значит, что кэширующий, логирующий или проверяющий права декоратор
      над `Get` не сработает для поиска, который выполняется внутри `GetAll`.

      Что можно сделать, если нужно перехватывать и внутренние вызовы:

      - реализовать `GetAll` в самом декораторе через его собственный `Get`, а не делегировать целиком;
      - вынести общую логику так, чтобы внутренний объект не вызывал сам себя через публичный контракт;
      - использовать наследование с `virtual`-методами: в подклассе с переопределённым `Get` вызов `Get(id)`

  en:
    title: How many Get calls does a decorator count when GetAll calls Get internally?
    prompt: |
      `CountingRepository` is a decorator that counts `Get` calls and passes them on to the wrapped repository.
      The `GetAll` method of `InMemoryRepository` calls its own `Get` three times internally. The program calls
      `GetAll` through the decorator reference. What does it print to the console?
    hint: Does `InMemoryRepository` know that it has been wrapped in another object?
    options:
      a: "0 3"
      b: "3 3"
      c: "3 0"
      d: "0 0"
    optionExplanations:
      b: "The inner `GetAll` calls `Get(id)`, that is `this.Get(id)`, and `this` there is the `InMemoryRepository`, not the decorator. The inner object has no reference to the decorator, so these calls bypass the decorator's counter."
      c: "A decorator does not replace the inner object, it delegates work to it: the decorator's `GetAll` calls `_inner.GetAll()`, and the inner `Get` runs three times, incrementing `inner.GetCalls`."
      d: "`InMemoryRepository.GetAll` really does call its own `Get` three times, and each call increments its own `GetCalls` counter, so the second number is 3."
    answer: "0 3"
    explanation: |
      A decorator intercepts only the calls that arrive through a reference to the decorator itself. The call
      `repo.GetAll()` reaches `CountingRepository.GetAll`, which passes it to `_inner.GetAll()`. From then on the
      code runs inside `InMemoryRepository`: the call `Get(id)` is `this.Get(id)`, where `this` points to the inner
      object. The decorator is no longer part of that path, so its counter stays at `0` and the inner object's
      counter reaches `3`.

      This is a limit of composition: the wrapped object does not know about its wrapper, and its calls to itself
      go around it. In practice a caching, logging or permission-checking decorator over `Get` does not apply to
      the lookups that happen inside `GetAll`.

      What you can do if internal calls must be intercepted too:

      - implement `GetAll` in the decorator itself on top of its own `Get` instead of delegating it as a whole;
      - restructure the code so that the inner object does not call itself through the public contract;
      - use inheritance with `virtual` methods: in a subclass that overrides `Get`, the call `Get(id)` from the
        base `GetAll` is dispatched to the override. The cost is tight coupling to the base class.
    linkTitles:
      - "Decorator pattern (Refactoring.Guru)"
      - "The this keyword"

locales:
  ru:
    title: Когда для процесса заказа стоит выбрать паттерн State вместо enum и switch-выражений?
    prompt: |
      Сервис заказов хранит статус заказа как enum, а переходы описаны в одном switch-выражении (код выше).
      Продукт просит добавить возвраты, частичную отгрузку и тайм-аут оплаты, и от статуса начинает зависеть
      всё больше операций: изменение адреса, добавление позиций, расчёт платы за отмену, выбор уведомлений.
      Коллега предлагает заменить enum паттерном State: интерфейс `IOrderState` и по классу на каждое состояние.

      Когда процесс заказа оправдывает паттерн State вместо enum со switch-выражениями и чего стоит каждый подход?
    hint: Посчитайте, сколько мест придётся менять при добавлении нового статуса и сколько - при добавлении новой операции, которая зависит от статуса.
    answer: |
      **Enum с явной таблицей переходов достаточно, когда:**

      - состояний немного и их набор стабилен, а для большинства операций статус отвечает только на вопросы
        «разрешено или нет» и «какой статус следующий»;
      - от статуса зависят одна-две операции, а не десяток.

      Сильные стороны: весь граф переходов виден в одном месте (его можно показать продукту и нарисовать
      диаграмму), в базе это обычный столбец с enum, каждую пару (статус, событие) легко покрыть табличным
      тестом, а все запрещённые переходы - это одна ветка `_ => throw`.

      **Цена enum по мере роста процесса:**

      - у каждой зависящей от статуса операции свой `status switch`, поэтому правила одного состояния (например,
        `Shipped`) размазаны по многим методам, и изменение одного состояния означает поиск по всем switch;
      - новый статус затрагивает все switch: switch-выражение без ветки `_` получит предупреждение компилятора
        CS8509 о необработанном значении, а switch с веткой `_` молча отправит новый статус в неё;
      - данные, которые имеют смысл только в некоторых состояниях (номер отправления, сумма возврата), живут
        nullable-полями заказа, а инварианты вида «заполнено только в `Shipped`» проверяются вручную.

      **State окупается, когда:**

      - многие операции не просто разрешены или запрещены, а ведут себя по-разному во многих состояниях, и
        одинаковый switch по статусу встречается во многих местах и меняется синхронно;
      - у состояний есть свои условия и данные: отмена из `Paid` считает плату и запускает возврат, а из
        `Placed` бесплатна;
      - набор состояний продолжает расти: новое состояние - это новый класс, и компилятор требует реализовать в
        нём все операции интерфейса.

      **Цена State:**

      - граф переходов распределён по классам: каждое состояние знает своих преемников, и ни одно место не
        показывает процесс целиком;
      - больше типов и косвенности; контекст должен открыть состояниям методы для своего изменения, либо каждая
        операция возвращает следующее состояние;
      - в базе всё равно хранится значение статуса, поэтому при загрузке заказа нужна фабрика, которая
        превращает сохранённый статус в объект состояния;
      - новая операция теперь затрагивает все классы состояний: баланс подхода с enum переворачивается.

      **Практическое решение:** начать с enum и явной таблицы переходов и переходить к State, когда число
      switch по статусу и история их изменений показывают, что правила одного состояния размазаны по коду. Даже
      тогда полезно держать переходы в одной таблице (или в библиотеке конечных автоматов), а в классах состояний -
      только поведение, чтобы граф оставался проверяемым. В обоих вариантах нужны табличные тесты по всем парам
      (статус, событие).
    explanation: |
      Выбор - это разновидность «проблемы выражений» (expression problem). При enum и switch новая операция
      стоит дёшево (ещё один метод со своим switch), а новое состояние - дорого (правка всех switch). В State
      наоборот: новое состояние - один класс, а новая операция - правка всех классов состояний. Поэтому решающий
      вопрос - что в этом процессе будет меняться чаще.

      Вторая ось - где живёт знание о переходах. Таблица переходов собирает его в одном месте: её легко читать,
      проверять и тестировать. В классическом State переходы распределены по классам, что удобно для поведения
      конкретного состояния, но скрывает общую картину. Refactoring.Guru прямо отмечает, что паттерн может быть
      избыточным, если состояний мало или они редко меняются.

      В коде выше ветка `_ => throw` в таблице переходов намеренная: любая не описанная пара - запрещённый
      переход. Но в switch-выражениях, где решается поведение по статусу, такая ветка опасна: она лишает вас
      предупреждения компилятора при добавлении нового значения enum, и новый статус молча получает поведение
      по умолчанию.

      - "State (Refactoring.Guru, английская версия)"
      - "Состояние (Refactoring.Guru)"
      - "Выражение switch"
  en:
    title: When should an order workflow use the State pattern instead of an enum with switch expressions?
    prompt: |
      An order service stores the order status as an enum and describes the transitions in one switch
      expression (code above). Product asks for refunds, partial shipments and payment timeouts, and more
      operations depend on the status: changing the address, adding items, calculating the cancellation fee,
      choosing notifications. A colleague proposes replacing the enum with the State pattern: an `IOrderState`
      interface and one class per state.

      When does an order workflow justify the State pattern instead of an enum with switch expressions, and what
      does each approach cost?
    hint: Count how many places change when you add a new status, and how many change when you add a new operation that depends on the status.
    answer: |
      **An enum with an explicit transition table is enough when:**

      - there are few states and the set is stable, and for most operations the status answers only "allowed or
        not" and "what is the next status";
      - one or two operations depend on the status, not ten.

      Strengths: the whole transition graph is visible in one place (you can show it to product and draw a
      diagram from it), the database stores a plain enum column, every (status, trigger) pair is easy to cover with
      a table-driven test, and all forbidden transitions are a single `_ => throw` arm.

      **What the enum costs as the workflow grows:**

      - every status-dependent operation gets its own `status switch`, so the rules of one state (say `Shipped`)
        are scattered over many methods, and changing one state means hunting through every switch;
      - a new status touches every switch: a switch expression without a `_` arm gets compiler warning CS8509
        about the unhandled value, while a switch with a `_` arm silently sends the new status into it;
      - data that makes sense only in some states (tracking number, refund amount) lives in nullable fields of
        the order, and invariants such as "set only in `Shipped`" are checked by hand.

      **State pays off when:**

      - many operations are not just allowed or forbidden but behave differently in many states, and the same
        switch over the status appears in many places and changes in lockstep;
      - states have their own conditions and data: cancelling from `Paid` calculates a fee and starts a refund,
        while cancelling from `Placed` is free;
      - the set of states keeps growing: a new state is a new class, and the compiler requires it to implement
        every operation of the interface.

      **What State costs:**

      - the transition graph is spread across classes: each state knows its successors, and no single place shows
        the whole workflow;
      - more types and indirection; the context has to expose methods that let states change it, or every
        operation returns the next state;
      - the database still stores a status value, so loading an order needs a factory that turns the stored status
        into a state object;
      - a new operation now touches every state class: the balance of the enum approach is reversed.

      **Practical decision:** start with an enum and an explicit transition table, and move to State when the
      number of switches over the status and their change history show that the rules of one state are smeared
      across the code. Even then it helps to keep the transitions in one table (or in a state machine library) and
      only the behaviour in the state classes, so the graph stays reviewable. Either way, write table-driven tests
      over all (status, trigger) pairs.
    explanation: |
      The choice is a form of the expression problem. With an enum and switches a new operation is cheap (one
      more method with its own switch) and a new state is expensive (edit every switch). With State it is the
      other way round: a new state is one class, and a new operation means editing every state class. So the
      deciding question is which of the two will change more often in this workflow.

      The second axis is where the knowledge of transitions lives. A transition table gathers it in one place:
      it is easy to read, review and test. In the classic State pattern transitions are distributed across the
      classes, which suits the behaviour of a specific state but hides the overall picture. Refactoring.Guru
      states plainly that the pattern can be overkill when there are only a few states or they rarely change.

      In the code above the `_ => throw` arm of the transition table is deliberate: any pair that is not listed
      is a forbidden transition. In switch expressions that decide behaviour by status, though, such an arm is
      dangerous: it removes the compiler warning when a new enum value is added, and the new status silently
      gets the default behaviour.
    linkTitles:
      - "State (Refactoring.Guru)"
      - "State (Refactoring.Guru, Russian version)"
      - "switch expression"

      запущенный отдельно, всегда проходит. Разбор показал, что в коде несколько десятков статических синглтонов
      (`PriceCache.Instance`, `Settings.Current` и подобные) и ambient-контекстов (статические `CurrentUser` и
      `TenantContext.Current`), а также прямые обращения к `DateTime.UtcNow`. Статические кэши и контексты
      хранят состояние между тестами.

      Часть команды предлагает зафиксировать порядок запуска тестов и отключить их параллельное выполнение.
      Вы техлид. Что вы решите и как организуете переход, не останавливая разработку новых функций?
    hint: |
      Чем время жизни статического поля отличается от времени жизни синглтона в DI-контейнере? И все ли из этих
      десятков мест на самом деле ломают тесты?
    answer: |
      1. **Решение: лечить причину, а не симптом.** Фиксированный порядок и отключённая параллельность только
         прячут связность тестов: следующий новый тест, фильтр в IDE или обновление test runner вернут падения, а
         прогон станет медленнее. Допустимо лишь временно, с владельцем и сроком, вынести несколько самых
         проблемных тестов в непараллельную группу, пока идёт миграция.
      2. **Остановить рост.** Договориться с командой и записать в инженерные правила: новое изменяемое
         статическое состояние и новые `static Instance` не принимаются. Подкрепить это механически: пункт в
         чек-листе code review, запрет обращений к статическим точкам доступа уже мигрированных классов через
         анализатор или архитектурный тест. Иначе статики появляются быстрее, чем их убирают.
      3. **Инвентаризация и приоритеты.** Составить список статиков и разделить их на группы. Неизменяемые и
         без состояния (константы, чистые вспомогательные функции) можно оставить. Изменяемые кэши и реестры,
         которых касаются тесты, и ambient-контексты (текущий пользователь, арендатор, часы) идут первыми.
         Связать их с падениями: прогнать набор тестов несколько раз и в случайном порядке и посмотреть, какое
         общее состояние затрагивают упавшие тесты. Порядок работы определяется вредом для тестов.
      4. **Переводить по одному, небольшими PR.** Для каждого статика: выделить интерфейс, зарегистрировать
         реализацию через `AddSingleton` в корне композиции, получать её через конструктор. Старый `Instance`
         пометить `[Obsolete]`, чтобы оставшиеся вызовы были видны как предупреждения, переводить вызывающий код
         постепенно и удалить статик, когда вызовов не останется. Не заменять статик статическим доступом к
         `IServiceProvider`: это service locator, и глобальное состояние никуда не девается.
      5. **Ambient-контексты превратить в явные зависимости.** Часы - `TimeProvider` (начиная с .NET 8) с
         фейковой реализацией в тестах. Текущий пользователь и арендатор - scoped-сервис, который заполняется на
         границе запроса. Статические словари-кэши - `IMemoryCache` или собственный сервис кэша,
         зарегистрированный в DI.
      6. **Учесть новые риски.** Синглтон из DI в production по-прежнему общий для всех запросов: он должен быть
         потокобезопасным и не должен захватывать scoped-сервисы (captive dependency). В разработке и тестах
         включить `ValidateScopes` и `ValidateOnBuild`. Каждый тест или фикстура строит свой контейнер или хост,
         поэтому экземпляры между тестами больше не разделяются.
      7. **Вести миграцию как проект.** Владелец, фиксированная доля каждого спринта, видимая метрика (сколько
         статиков осталось, доля нестабильных прогонов в CI), первые переводы в паре, чтобы команда освоила
         рецепт. Владельцу продукта объяснить пользу в его терминах: потерянное время на перезапуски CI и
         надёжность релизов.
    explanation: |
      Статическое поле живёт столько же, сколько процесс, поэтому его видят все тесты прогона. Результат теста
      начинает зависеть от того, что до него и параллельно с ним сделали другие тесты, отсюда и случайные
      падения. Синглтон в DI - это один экземпляр на контейнер. В production контейнер один, и поведение
      "один экземпляр на приложение" сохраняется. В тестах у каждого контейнера свой экземпляр, и состояние
      изолировано. Поэтому перевод на время жизни singleton в DI не меняет семантику в production, но
      возвращает тестам независимость. Рекомендации Microsoft по DI прямо советуют избегать статических классов
      и членов с состоянием и использовать вместо глобального состояния сервисы с временем жизни singleton.
      Refactoring.Guru среди недостатков паттерна Singleton называет трудности с модульным тестированием
      клиентского кода и то, что он маскирует плохой дизайн: зависимость не видна в сигнатуре класса.

      Подгонка порядка тестов плоха не только тем, что она хрупкая. Зависимость тестов от порядка - сама по
      себе дефект, и то же общее состояние часто даёт ошибки и в production, например кэш, который протекает
      между арендаторами или пользователями. Тесты здесь работают как ранний сигнал, и заглушать его опасно.

      Переписывать всё разом не стоит: десятки статиков, переход затрагивает много вызывающего кода, риск
      регрессий высокий, а разработка функций встанет. Статики без состояния тестам не мешают, поэтому
      приоритет по реальному вреду даёт большую часть выигрыша за малую часть работы. Задача лида - не только
      выбрать технический рецепт, но и сделать так, чтобы правило соблюдалось без его личного контроля: запрет
      на новые статики, проверка в инструментах, метрика и владелец.
    linkTitles:
      - "Рекомендации по внедрению зависимостей"
      - "Singleton (Refactoring.Guru, английская версия)"
      - "Одиночка (Refactoring.Guru)"
  en:
    title: "Tests fail randomly because of static singletons and ambient contexts: what does a tech lead decide and how is the migration run?"
    prompt: |
      In a large .NET solution the tests are flaky: the same run is green one time and red the next, and a
      failed test always passes when run on its own. The investigation shows several dozen static singletons
      (`PriceCache.Instance`, `Settings.Current` and the like) and ambient contexts (static `CurrentUser` and
      `TenantContext.Current`), plus direct calls to `DateTime.UtcNow`. The static caches and contexts keep
      state between tests.

      Part of the team proposes fixing the test execution order and switching off parallel test execution.
      You are the tech lead. What do you decide, and how do you run the transition without stopping feature work?
    hint: |
      How does the lifetime of a static field differ from the lifetime of a singleton in a DI container? And do
      all of those dozens of places actually break the tests?
    answer: |
      1. **Decision: fix the cause, not the symptom.** A fixed order and disabled parallelism only hide the
         coupling between tests: the next new test, a filter in the IDE or a test runner upgrade brings the
         failures back, and the run gets slower. At most, as a temporary measure with an owner and a date, move
         a few of the worst tests into a non-parallel group while the migration runs.
      2. **Stop the growth.** Agree with the team and write into the engineering guidelines that new mutable
         static state and new `static Instance` members are not accepted. Back it up mechanically: a code review
         checklist item, and a ban on the static accessors of already migrated classes through an analyzer or an
         architecture test. Otherwise statics appear faster than they are removed.
      3. **Inventory and prioritise.** List the statics and split them into groups. Immutable and stateless
         ones (constants, pure helper functions) can stay. Mutable caches and registries that tests touch, and
         ambient contexts (current user, tenant, clock), go first. Link them to failures: run the suite several
         times and in random order, and see which shared state the failing tests touch. The order of work is
         set by the damage to the tests.
      4. **Migrate one at a time, in small PRs.** For each static: extract an interface, register the
         implementation with `AddSingleton` in the composition root, receive it through constructors. Mark the old
         `Instance` as `[Obsolete]` so the remaining callers show up as warnings, migrate callers gradually and
         delete the static when no callers are left. Do not replace the static with static access to
         `IServiceProvider`: that is a service locator, and the global state stays.
      5. **Turn ambient contexts into explicit dependencies.** The clock becomes `TimeProvider` (.NET 8 and
         later) with a fake implementation in tests. The current user and tenant become a scoped service filled
         at the request boundary. Static dictionary caches become `IMemoryCache` or an own cache service
         registered in DI.
      6. **Watch the new risks.** A DI singleton is still shared by all requests in production: it must be
         thread-safe and must not capture scoped services (a captive dependency). Turn on `ValidateScopes` and
         `ValidateOnBuild` in development and tests. Each test or fixture builds its own container or host, so
         instances are no longer shared between tests.
      7. **Run the migration as a project.** An owner, a fixed share of every sprint, a visible metric (how
         many statics remain, the share of flaky CI runs), the first migrations done in pairs so the team learns
         the recipe. Explain the benefit to the product owner in their terms: time lost on CI reruns and release
         reliability.
    explanation: |
      A static field lives as long as the process, so every test in the run sees it. A test's result starts to
      depend on what other tests did before it and in parallel with it, hence the random failures. A DI
      singleton is one instance per container. In production there is one container, and the "one instance
      per application" behaviour is kept. In tests every container has its own instance, and the state is
      isolated. That is why moving to the DI singleton lifetime does not change production semantics but gives
      the tests their independence back. The Microsoft DI guidelines explicitly advise avoiding stateful static
      classes and members and using singleton services instead of global state. Refactoring.Guru lists among
      the drawbacks of the Singleton pattern that it makes client code hard to unit-test and that it can mask
      bad design: the dependency is not visible in the class signature.

      Tuning the test order is bad not only because it is fragile. A dependency of tests on their order is a
      defect in itself, and the same shared state often causes production bugs too, for example a cache that
      leaks between tenants or users. The tests are an early signal here, and silencing it is dangerous.

      Rewriting everything at once is not worth it: dozens of statics, the change touches a lot of calling
      code, the regression risk is high, and feature work would stop. Stateless statics do not hurt the tests,
      so prioritising by real damage gives most of the benefit for a small part of the work. The lead's job is
      not only to choose the technical recipe but to make the rule hold without personal policing: a ban on new
      statics, a check in the tooling, a metric and an owner.
    linkTitles:
      - "Dependency injection guidelines"
      - "Singleton (Refactoring.Guru)"
      - "Singleton (Refactoring.Guru, Russian version)"
